A 320g polar fleece mid-layer that holds heat, blocks wind and doesn't pill after a season of use — the layer you wear under a shell in winter and on its own in autumn.

Why we chose it

Most cheap fleece traps warmth and then soaks through the moment you work hard. This one is a soft-shell fleece: a windproof face over a brushed polar-fleece backing, so it stays warm on a ridge and still breathes on the climb. It's cut true to size, so it layers under a rain shell without bunching.

Details

  • 320g polar fleece, 100% polyester
  • Windproof soft-shell face, breathable backing
  • Anti-pilling and anti-static finish
  • Full zip, roughly 550g
  • Men's fit, S–3XL, six colours

Sizing

Cut true to size — take your usual. Shoulder width runs 39 cm (15.4 in) at S up to 49 cm (19.3 in) at 3XL, stepping 2 cm per size. If you plan to layer a thick base underneath, take the next size up.

Questions

Is a fleece warm enough for winter hiking? On its own it suits cool, dry days while you are moving. In cold, wet or windy weather, wear it over a base layer and under a waterproof shell, and carry an extra warm layer for stops.

Is it waterproof? No. The face blocks wind, but it is not a rain jacket. Add a waterproof shell in rain or wet snow.

What size should I get? It is cut true to size, so take your usual. Shoulder width runs from 39 cm (15.4 in) at S to 49 cm (19.3 in) at 3XL. If you wear a thick base layer underneath, take the next size up.

Is there a women's version? Yes, the Polar Fleece Soft-Shell Jacket for women, at the same price.

Backflush with clean water after each trip to clear the membrane. Let dry fully before storing. Don't let it freeze while wet — ice can crack the internal membrane.

Emergency use item. It buys time and warmth in a bad situation — it is not a replacement for a proper sleeping bag or shelter on a planned overnight.

Questions

Does an emergency bivy keep you warm? It helps you lose heat more slowly. The reflective lining sends body heat back to you and the shell blocks wind and rain, but it has no insulation of its own. It buys time in an emergency; it does not replace a sleeping bag.

How do I stay warmest inside it? Put on your dry layers and a hat first, then get something between you and the cold ground, such as a sit pad or your pack.

Why is it wet inside? The material is waterproof, so the moisture from your breath and body cannot get out and condenses inside. Keep your face out of the opening and leave the top a little open for air.

Can I use it again? If it is not torn, dry it and fold it loosely back into its bag. Check it for holes before each trip.

Most day hikes go fine with almost anything in your pack. The checklist matters for the ones that don't: the wrong turn that adds two hours, the storm that rolls in early, the twisted ankle a mile from the car. This is what experienced hikers carry on every day hike, why each item earns its place, and how much of it you actually need.

Quick answer: For a day hike, pack the Ten Essentials: navigation, a headlamp, sun protection, first aid, a knife or multi-tool, a fire starter, emergency shelter, extra food, extra water and an extra warm layer. Carry about 0.5 liters of water per hour of hiking, avoid cotton clothing, and tell someone your route and return time before you go.

Want it on paper? Download our free printable hiking checklist — 47 checks for before, during and after your hike, in US Letter, A4 and a phone version.

The Ten Essentials

The Ten Essentials are the classic safety list used by hiking clubs and park services. On a short, busy trail you won't use most of them. You carry them for the day something goes wrong.

1. Navigation

A map of the area, plus your route loaded on your phone or watch and downloaded for offline use. Cell signal disappears quickly in the mountains, but GPS keeps working. A GPX file of your route shows your position against the trail even in airplane mode.

2. Headlamp

Even on a morning hike. Most hikers who get caught out are simply slower than planned, and descending a rocky trail in the dark with a phone torch is how small problems become big ones. Pack spare batteries or a charged power bank.

3. Sun protection

Sunglasses, sunscreen and a hat. Exposed ridges and high elevations burn fast, even on cool days. A wide-brim hat shades your ears and neck, and a neck gaiter covers the rest.

4. First aid

Blister care, plasters, tape, pain relief, any personal medication and something to clean a cut. A compact trail first-aid kit covers the basics; add blister patches if you're breaking in boots.

5. Knife or multi-tool

For gear repairs, cutting tape or cord, and food prep. A small folding multi-tool handles most jobs.

6. Fire

A lighter or waterproof matches, for emergencies only. Check local fire restrictions before you go.

7. Emergency shelter

If you have to wait for help, staying warm and dry is what matters most. An emergency bivy weighs almost nothing and folds to the size of your palm.

8. Extra food

Pack more than you plan to eat: energy bars, nuts or trail mix. Eat small amounts often rather than one big lunch.

9. Extra water

Plan on about 0.5 liters per hour of hiking, more in heat or on steep climbs. A hydration backpack keeps water in reach so you actually drink, and a water filter straw lets you refill from streams on longer days.

10. Extra clothes

A warm layer and a shell, even in summer. Temperatures drop about 3.5°F for every 1,000 feet you climb, and the wind on a ridge feels nothing like the trailhead. A fleece and a packable windbreaker cover most conditions.

What to wear

  • No cotton next to your skin. Cotton stays wet and cold. Choose quick-dry synthetics or merino wool.
  • Hiking pants or shorts that stretch and dry fast, like our quick-dry trail shorts or trail pants.
  • Good socks. Merino wool socks are the cheapest upgrade against blisters.
  • Footwear with grip. Trail shoes are fine for most day hikes; boots help on rocky ground and with a heavier pack.

Comfort extras

  • Trekking poles take strain off your knees on long descents.
  • A foam sit pad makes every rest stop dry and warm.
  • A dry bag keeps your phone, layers and snacks dry in rain or at river crossings.
  • A small trash bag — pack out everything you bring in.

Before you leave the house

  1. Check the weather for the summit, not the town. Mountain forecasts are often very different.
  2. Check trail and road status. Closures and washouts won't show up in your weather app.
  3. Tell someone your route and your "back by" time.
  4. Charge your phone and download offline maps.
  5. Set a turnaround time and stick to it, even if the summit is in sight.

Day hike checklist summary

Safety Headlamp, first-aid kit, emergency bivy, knife or multi-tool, lighter, whistle
Clothing Quick-dry layers, warm fleece, wind or rain shell, hat, good socks
Sun Sunglasses, sunscreen, wide-brim hat
Extras Trekking poles, sit pad, dry bag, trash bag, charged phone

For overnight trips, multi-day hikes and cold or hot weather, our Ultimate Hiking Packing Checklist has six complete lists with quantities, and the Beginner Hiker Bundle adds the Beginner's Guide and a trip planner.

Frequently asked questions

How much water should I bring on a day hike?

Plan on about 0.5 liters per hour of hiking, and more in heat, at altitude or on steep climbs. A 4-hour hike needs roughly 2 liters. On longer routes, a water filter straw lets you refill from streams.

What size backpack do I need for a day hike?

A 15–25 liter daypack fits the Ten Essentials, water, food and a spare layer. A hydration pack with a built-in reservoir sleeve makes it easier to drink regularly.

What should I not wear hiking?

Avoid cotton next to your skin, including jeans and cotton T-shirts. Cotton stays wet and cold for hours. Choose quick-dry synthetics or merino wool, and never hike in brand-new footwear.

Do I need hiking boots for a day hike?

Not usually. Trail shoes with good grip work for most day hikes. Boots help on rocky, steep or wet terrain and when you carry a heavier pack.

What are the Ten Essentials for hiking?

Navigation, headlamp, sun protection, first aid, knife or multi-tool, fire, emergency shelter, extra food, extra water and extra clothes. They cover the most common ways a day hike goes wrong.

By the HikeSupply Co. team · October 28, 2026

In short: For most hikers, yes: trekking poles are worth it on steep descents, rough or slippery ground, stream crossings and long days with a pack, because they add balance and take some of the load off your legs and knees. On short, flat, smooth trails they matter much less, and you can hike fine without them. If you are unsure, start with one pole or an inexpensive pair and see whether you reach for them.

Trekking poles look like an optional extra, and plenty of hikers never use them. Others will not leave the trailhead without them. Here is what poles actually help with, where they do not, and how to decide for your own trails.

What do trekking poles actually do?

Poles give you two extra points of contact with the ground. REI's buying guide puts it simply: they enhance your stability and provide support on all types of terrain. In practice that means:

  • Better balance on loose gravel, roots, wet rock, mud and early-season ice patches.
  • Less load on your legs going downhill. Each pole plant takes a little of your weight through your arms instead of your knees and thighs.
  • A little help going uphill, since your arms can push you up steep sections.
  • Safer stream crossings, where a pole lets you test depth and footing before you step.

Do trekking poles help your knees?

There is research behind this one. A study in the Journal of Sports Sciences (1999), summarized by the New York-New Jersey Trail Conference, had volunteers walk down a 25-degree ramp carrying a pack of about 17 pounds, with and without two poles. With two poles, a key force on the knee was reduced by as much as 20 percent, and other knee forces dropped too. The biggest drop came when both poles were on the ground while one foot was in the air between steps.

That is a lab result on a steep ramp, not a promise for every trail or every knee. But it matches what many hikers feel on long descents: legs that are less shaky at the bottom. If you have a knee, hip or ankle problem, ask your doctor or physical therapist before relying on poles, and note that REI's guide says trekking poles are not a substitute for a medical cane.

Do trekking poles help going uphill?

Somewhat. A 2023 study from the University of Udine in Italy, published in the European Journal of Applied Physiology and reported by Backpacker, tested 15 trail runners on steep slopes. Outdoors, leg forces were about 5 percent lower with poles, and the runners climbed about 2.5 percent faster. The researchers' view was that poles help on steep climbs not because they save energy, but because they shift some of the work to your arms. On flat or rolling ground the benefit was less clear.

When are trekking poles not worth it?

Poles are not magic, and there are honest downsides:

  • Short, flat, smooth trails. On an easy 2-mile loop or a paved path, most people do not need them.
  • Scrambling. When you need your hands on rock, poles get in the way. Stow them on your pack first.
  • Busy or narrow trails. Poles take up space; keep them close to your body when passing other hikers.
  • Weight and fuss. They are one more thing to carry, adjust and keep track of.
  • Fragile ground. Metal tips can scratch rock and dig into soft soil. Stay on the trail and use rubber tip covers on rock or pavement if you have them.

Should you use one pole or two?

Trekking poles are usually sold and used as a pair, and the knee study above used two poles. Two poles give the most balance and the most load sharing on steep descents and with a heavy pack. One pole (or a hiking staff) works well on easier, fairly level trails with a light daypack, and leaves a hand free for a map, a camera or a dog leash. Many hikers start with one and add a second once they see the difference on a big downhill.

Quick guide: do you need trekking poles?

Your hike Poles? Why
Short, flat, smooth trail Optional Little to gain
